title: Fraud alert queue, June to September 2026

findings.headline: Nine in ten alerts are false positives
findings.detail: Only 313 of 3,000 alerts (10.4%) were confirmed fraud, so 89.6% of analyst effort went on genuine customers' alerts. Round-amount transfer (0.6% confirmed) and night-time login (1.6%) together make up 33.3% of alerts and rarely find fraud.

findings.headline: New device rule's fraud rate is rising month by month
findings.detail: Confirmed fraud under 'New device + high amount' went from 18.1% in Jun to 22.1%, 23.6% and 24.3% in Sep. It is 21.9% overall across 556 alerts, so it is a large, productive source of fraud.

findings.headline: Mule account and velocity rules are the best hit rates
findings.detail: 'Mule account inbound' confirms fraud in 31.7% of 243 alerts and 'Velocity' in 15.4% of 408. Mule alerts also take 21.2 minutes on average, against 11.4 overall, so they are costly but worthwhile.

findings.headline: Larger amounts and longer handling go with more fraud
findings.detail: The top fifth of alerts by amount (above 34,533) confirm fraud at 19.8%, against 3.7% for the lowest fifth. Alerts taking over 15 minutes confirm at 33.3%, but this probably reflects harder cases, not slower work.

findings.headline: Monthly fraud rate steady; analyst differences are modest
findings.detail: The monthly confirmed rate stayed between 9.7% and 11.1%, with no data gaps or duplicates. Among the eight analysts shown, rates run from 6.0% to 13.1%, which may reflect differing alert mix, so check before drawing conclusions.

next_steps: Review whether round-amount and night-time login rules can be tightened or down-prioritised, given confirmed rates of 0.6% and 1.6%.
Investigate why the new device rule's confirmed rate rose from 18.1% to 24.3%, and check whether volume or criteria changed.
Compare analyst rates after adjusting for rule mix before any performance conversation, and review prioritising amounts above 34,533.

findings.headline: Nine in ten alerts turn out to be false positives
findings.detail: Only 313 of 3,000 alerts (10.4%) were confirmed fraud, so 89.6% were false positives. Round-amount transfer (0.6% confirmed) and night-time login (1.6%) make up 33.3% of alerts (17.1% + 16.2%) and rarely find fraud.

findings.headline: New device rule's fraud rate is higher in later months
findings.detail: Confirmed fraud under 'New device + high amount' went from 18.1% in Jun to 22.1%, 23.6% and 24.3% in Sep. It is 21.9% overall across 556 alerts. Four months show a pattern, not a cause.

findings.headline: Mule account rule has the highest fraud rate, and takes longest
findings.detail: 'Mule account inbound' confirms fraud in 31.7% of 243 alerts, ahead of 'New device + high amount' (21.9%) and 'Velocity' (15.4% of 408). Mule alerts average 21.2 minutes against 11.4 overall.

findings.headline: Larger amounts and longer handling go with more fraud
findings.detail: The top fifth of alerts by amount (from 34,533) confirm fraud at 19.8%, against 3.7% for the lowest fifth. Alerts taking 15 minutes or more confirm at 33.3%. This shows an association only.

findings.headline: Monthly fraud rate steady; analyst rates differ somewhat
findings.detail: The monthly confirmed rate stayed between 9.7% and 11.1%, with no missing data or duplicates. Among the eight analysts shown (of 12), rates run from 6.0% to 13.1%. The other four are not shown.

next_steps: Review whether the round-amount and night-time login rules can be tightened or given lower priority, given confirmed rates of 0.6% and 1.6%.
Check whether the volume or criteria of the new device rule changed between June and September, as its confirmed rate rose from 18.1% to 24.3%.
Compare all 12 analysts' rates by rule before any performance discussion, and test whether amounts from 34,533 upwards should be triaged first.
conclusion: The queue is dominated by false positives (89.6%), and two rules making up a third of alerts almost never find fraud. Mule account and new device alerts find the most fraud. Start by reviewing the round-amount and night-time login rules, which would free analyst time for higher-yield alerts.
limits: This review uses summary statistics for one four-month period, so it cannot show why rates differ, whether analyst differences are fair, or what a rule change would do.
